templates.name: Principle plus case leads to consequence (S10 trade-off folded in)
Rule or timeline plus observation rejects a premise
Undercut leads to a hedged conclusion
X but not Y, so Z
Two cases or two accounts lead to a conditional or a common ground
Co-occurrence or repeated pattern leads to a link
Behaviour, design or content reveals a motive or belief (S12 example folded in)
Received view plus counterevidence leads to revision

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: words spoken versus words read silently in one study list
items.passage: When people study a list of words, does it help to say the words out loud? Psychologist Colin MacLeod and his research group at the University of Waterloo in Canada investigated this question. In one experiment, participants viewed a series of words on a screen, pronouncing some of them aloud and reading the others silently. Afterward, the participants were presented with a longer list of words and asked to identify which ones they had studied earlier. They correctly recognized more of the words they had pronounced than of the words they had read silently. This result suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: speaking certain words during study may make those words easier to recognize later.
people remember words better when they study in a quiet room than in a noisy one.
reading silently is the most effective way for students to learn the meanings of new words.
people who often read aloud can remember longer lists of words than people who rarely do.
items.explanation: Participants pronounced some words “aloud” and read “the others silently,” and later “correctly recognized more of the words they had pronounced than of the words they had read silently.” Since the only difference between the two sets of words was whether they were spoken, saying a word during study may make it easier to recognize later.

B.why_wrong: The study compared spoken and silent words, not quiet and noisy rooms, which the text never mentions.

C.why_wrong: The study tested recognition of studied words, not learning word meanings, and silent reading led to worse recognition, not better.

D.why_wrong: The experiment compared words within each participant’s list; it did not compare people who often read aloud with people who rarely do.

sources.what: MacLeod, Gopie, Hourihan, Neary, Ozubko 2010, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition (PubMed abstract): the production effect, producing a word aloud at study rather than reading it silently improves recognition, in mixed lists where some words are spoken; University of Waterloo

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology). S1 easy: one factor varied within a list (spoken vs silent), outcome recognition. Distractors: VAR, REC, CMP; D also matches the paper’s finding that the effect appears within mixed lists, not between people. Replaced the claimed damselfish noise subject (same species as a live w3 item).

items.subtype: T2 evaluation: a whole-school comparison reveals why within-school trials understated an effect
items.passage: Intestinal worms spread among children through soil contaminated by infected people, so treating some children can reduce infections even among other children who remain untreated. Earlier trials of deworming medication had compared randomly selected pupils within schools with their untreated classmates, but in Kenya, economists Edward Miguel and Michael Kremer instead assigned entire schools to begin treatment at different times. Absences declined by roughly a quarter in the participating schools, and untreated pupils in those schools also experienced fewer infections and attended more regularly than pupils at schools that had not yet begun the program. These results suggest that the earlier trials ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: may have underestimated the medication’s benefits, since the classmates used for comparison were themselves partly protected.
may have overestimated the medication’s benefits, since the pupils selected for treatment were likely healthier to begin with.
probably measured the medication’s effect on attendance accurately but overlooked its effect on pupils’ test scores.
may have exaggerated how much untreated pupils gained from the treatment of the classmates around them.
items.explanation: Earlier trials “compared randomly selected pupils within schools with their untreated classmates.” But Miguel and Kremer found that “untreated pupils in those schools also experienced fewer infections and attended more regularly” than pupils at untreated schools. If untreated classmates also benefit, comparing treated pupils with them makes the medication look less effective than it is, so the earlier trials may have understated its benefits.

B.why_wrong: The earlier trials treated “randomly selected pupils,” so there is no basis for thinking the treated pupils were healthier to begin with.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about test scores, and its findings suggest the earlier trials misjudged even the effect on attendance, since their comparison pupils also benefited.

D.why_wrong: Trials that compared treated pupils with their own classmates could not measure what those classmates gained; the new results show the untreated pupils gained, so that benefit was missed, not exaggerated.

sources.what: Miguel and Kremer, NBER Working Paper 8481 (Econometrica 2004): mass school deworming cut absenteeism in treatment schools by one quarter; health and participation benefits for untreated children in treatment schools and neighboring schools; earlier within-school randomized trials may have understated effects

items.notes: Area: social science (development economics, health). S1 hard: a comparison of schools hidden behind a design question; two steps (untreated classmates benefit; so a within-school comparison shrinks the measured gain). Distractors: CAUSE (selection), OUT (test scores), REV (spillover exaggerated).

band7.why: Two steps (spillover protects untreated classmates; so a within-school comparison shrinks the measured gain). The principle is stated in the first sentence, which helps; B (selection bias) is answered by "randomly selected", D reverses the direction of the spillover error, C keeps attendance and adds test scores. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: a nest experiment rules out the parasite explanation but shows another benefit
items.passage: European starlings weave fresh, strongly aromatic herbs into the otherwise dry grass of their nests, and one proposed explanation for this behavior is that compounds in the herbs repel the mites, lice, and fleas that feed on nestlings. To test this hypothesis, Helga Gwinner and colleagues replaced 148 starling nests with artificial ones, half containing herbs and half containing only grass. The parasite loads in the two kinds of nests proved indistinguishable. Nestlings raised among herbs, however, weighed more and had a higher proportion of red blood cells when they fledged, and more of them were observed at the colony the following year. The researchers therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: starlings add herbs to their nests mainly so that they can locate those nests by smell.
the herbs likely aid nestlings in some way other than by reducing parasites.
the herbs repel parasites only in nests that starlings have constructed themselves.
nestlings in grass nests were more likely than those in herb nests to survive their first year.
items.explanation: The idea that herbs “repel the mites, lice, and fleas” failed the test, since parasite loads in the two kinds of nests “proved indistinguishable.” Yet nestlings raised among herbs “weighed more,” had more red blood cells, and were seen at the colony more often the next year. The herbs therefore seem to help nestlings by some route other than cutting parasites.

A.why_wrong: The text never suggests starlings use the herbs to find their nests; the study tested only parasites and nestling condition.

C.why_wrong: The study used artificial nests, so it shows nothing about natural nests; this is a guess that would rescue the parasite idea without any support in the text.

D.why_wrong: More nestlings from herb nests “were observed at the colony the following year,” which points the other way.

sources.what: Gwinner, Oltrogge, Trost, Nienaber 2000, Animal Behaviour (PubMed abstract): 148 starling nests replaced with artificial nests with herbs or grass; ectoparasite loads indistinguishable; herb nestlings heavier with higher haematocrit at fledging; more herb yearlings seen in the colony next year; herbs improve condition but do not reduce parasites

items.notes: Area: natural science (ornithology). S1 medium: herbs vs grass, parasites equal but nestlings better off, so the parasite explanation fails and another benefit remains. Distractors: CAUSE (smell to find nests), EXT (natural nests only), REV (survival).

items.subtype: T4 explanation: isotope evidence rules out the outsider account of anti-vampire burials
items.passage: In seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Poland, some of the dead were buried with a sickle across the throat or a stone beneath the chin to keep them from rising as vampires. One hypothesis held that the six individuals given such burials at the Drawsko cemetery were immigrants. But when bioarchaeologist Lesley Gregoricka’s team analyzed strontium in their tooth enamel, which forms during childhood and reflects local geology, all six matched the local values found in the cemetery’s ordinary burials, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the practice of guarding against the dead most likely reached Drawsko with newcomers from other regions.
the six had grown up elsewhere but lived at Drawsko long enough for their teeth to take on its chemical signature.
nothing about these six people, including where they had come from, explains why the community feared that they would rise.
something other than an origin outside the community probably marked these six people as dangerous.
items.explanation: One hypothesis held that the six “were immigrants,” but their enamel, “which forms during childhood and reflects local geology,” matched “the local values found in the cemetery’s ordinary burials.” The six therefore grew up locally, so whatever led the community to fear them was most likely something other than their being outsiders.

A.why_wrong: The text examines only where the six people grew up; it offers no evidence about where the custom itself came from.

B.why_wrong: Enamel “forms during childhood,” so it records where a person grew up, not where an adult later lived; a local match points to a local childhood.

C.why_wrong: The strontium results rule out only one explanation, an origin outside the community; they say nothing about other traits of the six, such as how they died, so they cannot show that nothing about the six explains their burials.

sources.what: Gregoricka et al. 2014, PLoS ONE (PMC): six deviant burials at Drawsko 1 (17th to 18th c.), sickles across the throat or abdomen, stones beneath chins; hypothesis that they were non-local immigrants tested with enamel strontium; all six local, so something other than origin marked them

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S11, hard T4: a hypothesis (outsiders) undercut by isotope evidence; two steps (enamel records childhood residence; a local match rules out the outsider account, so another cause is needed). Distractors: CAUSE (origin of the custom), MIX (enamel read as adult residence), OUT (migrants’ burials). The paper’s own alternative (cholera victims) is left out so the key stays general.

fixes: C (OUT, migrants buried in ordinary graves; ruled out on sight) replaced by an EXT option that keeps the true premise (not outsiders) and overreaches to "nothing about these six"

band7.why: Two steps (enamel forms in childhood, so a local match means a local upbringing; that removes the outsider account, so another cause is needed). After the fix two wrong options are partly right: B keeps residence at Drawsko but breaks the childhood link, C keeps "not outsiders" but overreaches; A is a CAUSE on the custom. Key paraphrased ("marked ... as dangerous"). Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 with a doubt frame: a medieval critic’s account undercuts the view of the kharja as an ending ornament
items.passage: Many muwashshahs, strophic poems composed in al-Andalus in classical Arabic or Hebrew, conclude with a kharja, a final couplet frequently written in everyday Andalusi Arabic or in the Romance speech of the region. Because the kharja comes last and often switches languages, it could easily be mistaken for a decorative ending. However, the Egyptian writer Ibn Sanāʾ al-Mulk (1155–1211) stated that poets constructed the muwashshah from the kharja, and he considered borrowing an excellent kharja preferable to composing a poor one. His remarks challenge the assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: poets regarded the kharja as the most important part of the muwashshah.
the kharja was an afterthought, added only after the body of the poem had been written.
Romance was spoken in al-Andalus alongside Arabic and Hebrew.
muwashshahs were composed more often in classical Arabic than in Hebrew.
items.explanation: The kharja “could easily be mistaken for a decorative ending,” but Ibn Sanāʾ al-Mulk “stated that poets constructed the muwashshah from the kharja.” If poets built the poem from the kharja, it came first in the process of composition, which challenges the idea that it was an afterthought added once the rest of the poem was done.

A.why_wrong: Ibn Sanāʾ al-Mulk’s remarks support the idea that poets valued the kharja highly; the frame asks for an assumption the remarks challenge.

C.why_wrong: The text itself mentions “the Romance speech of the region,” and nothing in the remarks casts doubt on it.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares how often muwashshahs were written in Arabic and in Hebrew, and the remarks concern the kharja, not the poems’ languages.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Kharja: the kharja is the final couplet of a muwashshah (strophic poem of al-Andalus) in literary Arabic or Hebrew, often in vernacular Andalusi Arabic or Romance; Ibn Sana al-Mulk (1155 to 1211) said poets generated the muwashshah from the kharja and that borrowing a good kharja was better than composing a bad one

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature). S11 medium with a negative frame (as in 2.4, worded differently): a plausible reading of the kharja as an ending ornament, undercut by a medieval theorist; the key states the view undercut. Distractors: POL (what the remarks support), REP (a stated premise), CMP.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: fear of predators applied to islands that lost their large carnivores
items.passage: Large predators can affect an ecosystem even when they kill nothing, since prey animals that sense danger typically spend less time feeding. On British Columbia’s Gulf Islands, where most large carnivores have been eliminated, raccoons forage along the shore with little to fear. When biologist Justin Suraci’s team broadcast recordings of large carnivores’ calls along sections of shoreline for a month, raccoons there spent far less time foraging, and the intertidal crabs and fish they eat became considerably more abundant. These results suggest that the islands’ loss of large carnivores ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: may have reduced the numbers of crabs and fish on their shores even if it did not lead to any increase in the number of raccoons.
has let raccoons become so numerous that the crabs and fish they eat could not recover even if the raccoons foraged less.
has made raccoons quick to react to any unfamiliar sound, so recordings of harmless animals would likely reduce their foraging just as much.
has affected the shore’s crabs and fish mainly because those carnivores once competed with raccoons for the same prey.
items.explanation: Recordings kill nothing, yet when the team “broadcast recordings of large carnivores’ calls,” raccoons “spent far less time foraging,” and “the intertidal crabs and fish they eat became considerably more abundant.” Fear alone, with no change in how many raccoons there were, changed the prey. So losing the carnivores, and with them the raccoons’ fear, may have cut crab and fish numbers even without more raccoons.

B.why_wrong: The text reports that the crabs and fish did become more abundant once raccoons foraged less, so they were able to recover.

C.why_wrong: The text says raccoons forage “with little to fear” and reports only carnivore calls; nothing suggests they would react as strongly to the sounds of harmless animals.

D.why_wrong: The carnivores did matter to the shore, but the text traces their effect to the fear they cause raccoons, not to any competition for crabs and fish.

sources.what: Suraci, Clinchy, Dill, Roberts, Zanette 2016, Nature Communications (PMC): Gulf Islands, most large carnivores extirpated; month-long playbacks of large carnivore (dog) calls cut raccoon foraging by 66%; intertidal crabs, fish and worms increased; behaviour changed, not raccoon numbers

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). S2, T3: the principle (fear reduces feeding without killing) applied to islands that lost their carnivores; two steps (the playback changed behaviour only, not raccoon numbers; so the carnivores’ loss can matter through behaviour alone). Distractors: REV (crabs could not recover), CMP (harmless sounds, never tested in the passage), CAUSE (competition). The paper’s predator playback was domestic dog calls, the control pinniped calls; the passage keeps the abstract’s “large carnivore vocalizations.”

band7.why: Two steps (the playback changed behaviour, not raccoon numbers; so the carnivores' loss can lower prey through behaviour alone). Key paraphrased with an "even if" clause; B falls to the recovery result, C and D are rival readings (any sound, competition) that need the text to reject. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: the gambler’s fallacy applied to asylum rulings
items.passage: The gambler’s fallacy is the mistaken belief that random outcomes balance out over short sequences, so that after several coin tosses in a row land heads, tails seems overdue. Economists Daniel Chen, Tobias Moskowitz, and Kelly Shue found that decisions by US immigration judges ruling on a series of asylum applications exhibited precisely the pattern this fallacy would produce—a pattern unrelated to the merits of the cases and most pronounced among less experienced judges. An applicant whose case immediately follows several approvals by the same judge would therefore be likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: receive a favorable ruling, since a judge who has approved several cases in a row has shown a general willingness to grant asylum.
be judged solely on the merits of the case, provided that the judge has many years of experience.
have the decision reviewed by another judge, since streaks of identical rulings draw attention to a judge’s record.
face worse odds of being granted asylum than an applicant with an equally strong case heard after several denials.
items.explanation: Under the gambler’s fallacy, “after several coin tosses in a row land heads, tails seems overdue.” The text says the judges’ decisions “exhibited precisely the pattern this fallacy would produce,” one “unrelated to the merits of the cases.” A judge who has just approved several cases would thus lean toward denying the next one, so that applicant would likely fare worse than an equally strong applicant whose case followed denials.

A.why_wrong: This reasons from the judge’s record to leniency, but the fallacy the judges showed makes a run of approvals push the next ruling toward denial, not approval.

B.why_wrong: The pattern was “most pronounced among less experienced judges,” which means it was weaker among experienced ones, not that it disappeared.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about rulings being reviewed by other judges; it describes only how a judge’s rulings relate to the ones before them.

sources.what: Chen, Moskowitz, Shue, NBER Working Paper 22026 (QJE 2016): negative autocorrelation in asylum decisions unrelated to case merits, attributed to the gambler’s fallacy; stronger after streaks and among moderate and less experienced judges

items.notes: Area: social science (economics, law). S2, T3: the fallacy applied to a judge, then to an applicant; two steps (approvals make a denial seem due; so the next applicant fares worse than an equal one after denials). Distractors: REV (lenient-judge reasoning), EXT (weaker read as none), OUT (review). No percentages, since the abstract gives none.

band7.why: Two steps (approvals make a denial seem due; so the next applicant fares worse than an equal one after denials). A is a tempting reversal from the judge's record, B an EXT on the experience finding, C OUT. Key states the comparison the fallacy implies, not the passage's words. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: how multiple-language versions were made, applied to whether a version is the same film or a new one
items.passage: Silent films could be prepared for international audiences simply by translating their printed intertitles, but the introduction of synchronized sound in the late 1920s made spoken dialogue a considerable obstacle. Beginning in 1929, American and European studios frequently produced multiple-language versions: a film was shot in one language and then reshot on identical sets, with the same crew and costumes, by performers fluent in another language, and the screenplay was occasionally revised, with scenes inserted or eliminated. Drácula (1931), a Spanish-language version of Dracula, is among the relatively few such versions that survive. Given these practices, a multiple-language version ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: was more likely than the original-language film to survive, since studios made more copies of versions intended for export.
is difficult to classify either as simply another version of the original film or as a separate film in its own right.
carried the silent era’s practice of translated intertitles into the era of synchronized sound.
should be regarded as the same film as the original, since it was shot on the same sets with the same crew and costumes.
items.explanation: The text says each film was “reshot on identical sets, with the same crew and costumes,” but “by performers fluent in another language,” and that “the screenplay was occasionally revised, with scenes inserted or eliminated.” A version that shares so much with the original yet differs in cast and even in scenes is hard to classify: it is neither simply the same film nor clearly a different one.

A.why_wrong: The text says Drácula is “among the relatively few such versions that survive,” and it says nothing about studios making more copies of export versions.

C.why_wrong: Translated intertitles belong to silent film; multiple-language versions met the problem of dialogue by reshooting with new performers, not by continuing that practice.

D.why_wrong: The shared sets, crew, and costumes are only half the picture: each version had different performers, and its screenplay was sometimes revised “with scenes inserted or eliminated,” so the practices give just as much reason to call it a separate film.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Multiple-language version: from 1929 studios reshot films in several languages on the same sets with the same crew and costumes but different actors, scripts sometimes changed; whether they are one film or separate films is open to debate; few survive, Drácula (1931) among them

items.notes: Area: humanities (film history). S2, T3: the production practice (shared sets, crew and costumes; different casts and sometimes scenes) applied to what kind of thing a version is; two steps (the shared production points to the same film, the new cast and scenes to a different one; so it fits neither label cleanly). The source notes that this question is open to debate. Distractors: REV (survival), MIX (intertitles moved into the sound era), MIX (differences pinned on the shared sets).

fixes: D (sets and costumes differed; killed by "identical sets") replaced by a PART option that keeps the shared sets, crew and costumes and ignores the new cast and revised scenes

band7.why: Two steps (shared production points to one film, new cast and scenes to another, so neither label fits). After the fix D is a half-evidence option built on true premises; A still falls to the survival sentence and C is a plain MIX. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a poetic device of double meaning applied to poems about the powerful
items.passage: Qene, a form of improvised poetry traditionally taught in schools of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, depends on a literary device called sem-ena-werq, or “wax and gold.” The name derives from a goldsmithing technique in which wax is drained from a clay mold so that molten gold can replace it: a qene line presents an obvious interpretation, the wax, while ambiguous wordplay conceals a deeper significance, the gold. Because secular qene historically served to ridicule individuals in positions of authority, the device would have enabled a poet to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: criticize a powerful figure while offering a harmless surface reading that the poet could claim was the intended one.
make a hidden message obvious to every listener, since the wordplay involved was taught in the church’s schools.
mock several powerful people in a single line, since each of them could recognize himself in its wax.
praise a ruler through the wax of a poem while reserving its gold for the religious lessons taught in the church.
items.explanation: In qene, “a qene line presents an obvious interpretation, the wax, while ambiguous wordplay conceals a deeper significance, the gold,” and secular qene “historically served to ridicule individuals in positions of authority.” A poet could therefore place the ridicule in the hidden gold and point to the innocent wax if challenged, criticizing the powerful while keeping a safe surface meaning.

B.why_wrong: The device works because wordplay “conceals” the deeper meaning; making the message obvious to everyone would defeat that purpose.

C.why_wrong: The wax is the obvious interpretation, so mockery placed there would be open; the concealed meaning is the gold.

D.why_wrong: The text ties the device to secular poems that ridicule authority, not to praise in the wax and religious teaching in the gold.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Qene: improvised poetry developed in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and taught in its schools; sem-ena-werq (wax and gold), obvious meaning over a hidden one, named from lost-wax goldsmithing; secular qene used to subtly insult and criticize those in authority

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature). S2, T3: the double-meaning device applied to poems that ridicule the powerful; two steps (the ridicule can sit in the hidden layer; the harmless surface gives cover). Distractors: REV (obvious), MIX (layers swapped), MIX (praise and religious lessons).

band7.why: Two steps (ridicule sits in the hidden gold; the harmless wax gives the poet cover). B reverses the concealment, C and D swap the layers or the purpose; each needs the wax/gold mapping to reject. Strongest hard item in the batch. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a bullion economy applied to a trader paying for a small purchase
items.passage: Throughout much of Viking-age Scandinavia, silver functioned as currency by weight rather than by count. Hoards from the period combine complete coins from distant mints with ingots and hacksilver—fragments of jewelry and tableware that were deliberately chopped and bent—and archaeologists have also recovered Viking balance scales along with their accompanying weights. A trader possessing only a substantial foreign coin who intended to purchase goods worth less than the silver it contained would therefore most likely have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: exchanged it for smaller foreign coins, since hoards from the period contain complete coins from distant mints.
kept the coin whole, since cutting it would have destroyed the stamp that gave it its value.
traded it for an ingot of the same size, since the value of silver was set by its size rather than its weight.
paid with a piece cut from the coin, accepted for the amount of silver it contained.
items.explanation: The text says silver “functioned as currency by weight rather than by count” and describes hacksilver, “fragments of jewelry and tableware that were deliberately chopped and bent,” along with balance scales and weights. Since a coin’s worth lay in its silver, a trader needing to pay less than a whole coin’s value could most likely cut off a piece and have it weighed.

A.why_wrong: Hoards do contain complete foreign coins, but the text says silver passed “by weight rather than by count” and describes silver “deliberately chopped and bent”; nothing mentions smaller coins being available, so the evidence points to cutting the coin, not swapping it.

B.why_wrong: Silver “functioned as currency by weight rather than by count,” so a coin’s value did not depend on its stamp, and chopped silver was in common use.

C.why_wrong: The text says silver was valued by weight, not by size, so an ingot of the same size would not necessarily match the coin’s value.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Hacksilver: cut and bent silver used as bullion or currency by weight; common among the Vikings; hoards mix hacksilver, coins, ingots and jewellery; a Viking weighing scale with weights found on the Isle of Gigha

items.notes: Area: history (Viking-age economy). S2, T3: the principle (silver valued by weight) applied to a trader paying less than a whole coin’s worth; two steps (value lay in the metal; so a cut piece could pay). Distractors: OUT (local mints), REV (the stamp gives value), MIX (size for weight).

fixes: A (OUT, local mint coins easier to weigh) replaced by an option that keeps a true premise (hoards hold complete coins from distant mints) and draws the count-based conclusion the text rules out

band7.why: Two steps (value lay in weight, and chopped silver and scales show pieces were weighed; so a fraction of a coin could be cut and weighed). After the fix A rests on a true hoard fact; B and C still fall to "by weight rather than by count". Short passage (77 words); band 6 near its easy edge.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: projected translations resolve an opera company’s trade-off
items.passage: An opera company performing for audiences unfamiliar with a work’s original language traditionally confronted a dilemma. It could present the work in translation, altering the words the composer had originally set to music, or retain the original language and leave many listeners unable to comprehend the libretto. In January 1983, the Canadian Opera Company staged Richard Strauss’s Elektra with English translations of the libretto projected above the stage, one of the earliest uses of surtitles in a live performance. Surtitles would thus enable a company to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: present operas in translation more often, since audiences would grow accustomed to reading the composers’ original words.
let singers perform in the audience’s own language while the composer’s original words are projected above the stage.
avoid the expense of hiring singers capable of performing in several different languages.
present a work in the language its composer set to music while still letting the audience understand the words.
items.explanation: A company had to choose between “altering the words the composer had originally set to music” and leaving “many listeners unable to comprehend the libretto.” Surtitles project “English translations of the libretto” above the stage, so the singers can keep the original language while the audience reads what the words mean.

A.why_wrong: Surtitles remove the need to sing in translation, so they would let companies perform in translation less often, not more.

B.why_wrong: This reverses the roles: the company projected “English translations of the libretto” above the stage so that the singers could keep the original words; with surtitles the singing is not translated.

C.why_wrong: The text never discusses the cost of hiring singers; the dilemma it describes concerns what audiences can understand.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Surtitles: translated lyrics projected above a stage; Lotfi Mansouri of the Canadian Opera Company used them for the first time in a live performance in the January 1983 staging of Elektra

items.notes: Area: humanities (music, theater). S2 medium, T3: a trade-off (translation vs comprehension) plus a new tool leads to the consequence; two steps (projected translations supply understanding; so the original language can stay). Distractors: REV, MIX (direction of translation), OUT (cost). Elektra is by Richard Strauss (1909); the source names the production, not the language sung, so the passage says only that English translations were projected.

fixes: B ("perform operas written in English for audiences abroad without translating their librettos") was a defensible special case of the key (an English opera abroad with local-language surtitles); replaced by a MIX that swaps what is sung and what is projected

items.subtype: T1 dating: the latest tree ring sets the earliest possible date of an object
items.passage: Trees add one growth ring each year, so the rings in a piece of old wood can reveal approximately when the tree it came from was growing. In 2005, researchers used this method, called dendrochronology, to examine an oak door at Westminster Abbey in London. The rings preserved in the door’s planks span the years 924 to 1030. Because the planks’ outermost layers had been trimmed away when the door was constructed, the researchers could not determine precisely when the tree was felled. Still, these findings indicate that the door ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: was made from a tree that was cut down in the year 924.
is more recent than any other door in Westminster Abbey.
could not have been made before the year 1030.
was repaired with new wood sometime around the year 1030.
items.explanation: The rings “span the years 924 to 1030,” so the tree was still growing in 1030 and could not have been cut down before then. A door made from its planks therefore could not have been built before 1030, even though the exact year the tree “was felled” cannot be known.

A.why_wrong: The year 924 is when the rings begin, not when the tree was cut; the tree was still growing in 1030.

B.why_wrong: The text discusses only this one door and gives no dates for any other door in the abbey.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about repairs; 1030 is simply the year of the last ring preserved in the planks.

sources.what: Westminster Abbey, Britain’s oldest door: dated in 2005 by dendrochronology; rings show growth from AD 924 to 1030; bark trimmed when the planks were made, so the felling year is unknown (after 1032); door made in the 1050s

items.notes: Area: history (medieval England, dating). S3 easy: a rule (the last ring marks a year the tree was alive) plus the observation (rings to 1030) rules out an earlier date. Replaced the claimed ice-patch subject, whose logic repeated official 2.16.

items.subtype: T1 modus tollens: a sulfate record in both hemispheres rules out a high-latitude volcano
items.passage: Large volcanic eruptions deposit sulfate that is preserved in layers of polar ice. Sulfate from an eruption near the equator can spread into both hemispheres, whereas sulfate from an eruption at high latitudes generally remains within the volcano’s own hemisphere. Ice cores from both Greenland and Antarctica record an enormous sulfate deposit from an eruption around 1257, so even before geographer Franck Lavigne’s team traced it to the Samalas volcano in Indonesia, researchers could reasonably conclude that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the eruption had not occurred at a volcano far from the equator, such as one in Iceland.
the volcano lay in the Southern Hemisphere, since more of its sulfate would have remained south of the equator.
volcanoes near the equator erupt more often than volcanoes at high latitudes do.
the sulfate from the eruption had reached Greenland before it reached Antarctica.
items.explanation: Sulfate from an eruption “at high latitudes generally remains within the volcano’s own hemisphere,” but the 1257 sulfate appears in ice “from both Greenland and Antarctica.” A deposit in both hemispheres fits an eruption near the equator, so researchers could rule out a volcano far to the north or south, such as one in Iceland.

B.why_wrong: Sulfate staying in one hemisphere is what the text expects of a high-latitude eruption; this sulfate reached both, which points to the equator, not to the Southern Hemisphere.

C.why_wrong: The text concerns where sulfate spreads, not how often volcanoes in different regions erupt.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when the sulfate arrived at each ice sheet, only that both record it.

sources.what: Lavigne et al. 2013, PNAS (PubMed abstract): polar ice cores record a colossal eruption around 1257, most probably tropical, with sulfate in both Arctic and Antarctic records; the source identified as Samalas volcano, Lombok, Indonesia

Wikipedia, 1257 Samalas eruption (research history): the sulfate layer was found in Greenland ice; a volcano near Greenland was first considered, but in 1988 Antarctic cores (Byrd Station, South Pole) were found to hold it too, and the source was placed close to the equator

items.notes: Area: natural science (volcanology, climate). S3 medium: a rule (high-latitude sulfate stays in its hemisphere) plus an observation (sulfate in both polar records) rejects a high-latitude source. The rule (tropical eruptions deposit sulfate at both poles, high-latitude ones mainly in their own hemisphere) is standard ice-core volcanology; the abstract states the conclusion it supports (ice cores show the 1257 eruption was most probably tropical). Distractors: MIX (rule misapplied), CMP (eruption frequency), OUT (timing).

fixes: added a second source that states the hinge premise (a signal in both Greenland and Antarctic ice led researchers away from a volcano near Greenland toward one near the equator); the PubMed abstract gives only the conclusion

items.subtype: T4 explanation: with stocking and stream links excluded, an experiment supports transport inside birds
items.passage: Fish appear in isolated ponds and lakes worldwide that no stream connects to other waters and that no one has stocked. Waterbirds have long been suspected of transporting fish eggs attached to their feet or feathers, but empirical support for that route is lacking, and the only fish eggs previously known to survive passage through a bird’s digestive tract were the resistant, dormant eggs of killifish. When Ádám Lovas-Kiss and colleagues fed developing eggs of common carp and Prussian carp to captive mallards, approximately 0.2% survived and some subsequently hatched, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: waterbirds carry far more fish eggs on their feet and feathers than inside their digestive tracts.
fish without hardy eggs might occasionally reach isolated waters inside ducks that have eaten their eggs.
developing fish eggs survive passage through a duck’s gut about as often as the dormant eggs of killifish do.
most of the fish found in isolated ponds probably descend from eggs that mallards carried there.
items.explanation: The text rules out streams and stocking for these waters, notes that support for eggs carried “attached to their feet or feathers” is lacking, and says only the “resistant, dormant eggs of killifish” were known to survive a bird’s gut. Carp eggs, which are “developing” rather than dormant, also passed through mallards alive and “some subsequently hatched,” so even fish without especially tough eggs might sometimes reach isolated waters inside ducks.

A.why_wrong: The text says “empirical support for that route is lacking,” so it gives no basis for saying birds carry more eggs externally than internally.

C.why_wrong: The study fed mallards only carp eggs and the text gives no survival rate for killifish eggs, which it calls “resistant,” so it offers no basis for saying the two kinds of eggs survive equally often.

D.why_wrong: Only about 0.2% of the eggs survived, and the study shows the route is possible, not that it explains most fish in isolated ponds.

sources.what: Lovas-Kiss et al. 2020, PNAS (PubMed abstract): fish colonize isolated waters without human help; external transport on feet and feathers long speculated but lacking empirical support; only resistant diapause killifish eggs known to survive gut passage; developing common carp and Prussian carp eggs fed to mallards, 0.2% survived, live embryos hatched

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). S4: routes into isolated waters narrowed (no streams, no stocking, external transport unsupported), then the experiment opens the internal route for ordinary eggs; two steps (carp eggs are not dormant like killifish eggs; they still survived, so ordinary fish could be carried inside birds). The passage says support is lacking, not that the external route is impossible, matching the source. Distractors: CMP, CMP, EXT.

fixes: C ("killifish eggs are more likely than carp eggs to survive ..., since they are dormant") was close to defensible, since the passage calls killifish eggs "resistant"; replaced by an equal-survival CMP that the text does not support and its wording points against

band7.why: Two steps (only dormant killifish eggs were known to survive; developing carp eggs also survived and hatched, so ordinary fish could travel inside birds). A and C are CMPs on true premises, D an EXT that keeps the route but inflates its share. Key paraphrased ("fish without hardy eggs"). Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 elimination: two possible sources of a snake’s toxins, one ruled out
items.passage: The Asian snake Rhabdophis tigrinus defends itself with glands on its neck that contain bufadienolides, toxic steroids also found in toads, which form part of the snake’s diet. The snake might either synthesize these compounds itself or obtain them from its prey. Investigating this question, biologist Deborah Hutchinson and her coauthors found that snakes collected from localities without toads lacked the toxins in their neck glands entirely, and in feeding experiments, hatchlings possessed the toxins only if they had been fed toads or their mother carried high concentrations of the compounds. The researchers therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: R. tigrinus likely acquires its toxins from toads, directly or via its mother, rather than making them.
R. tigrinus snakes living where toads are absent synthesize their own toxins to compensate for the missing prey.
hatchlings fed toads accumulated greater amounts of toxins than their mothers had.
R. tigrinus hatchlings can digest toads only if their mothers passed toxins to them before hatching.
items.explanation: The snake “might either synthesize these compounds itself or obtain them from its prey.” Snakes from localities without toads “lacked the toxins in their neck glands entirely,” and hatchlings had them “only if they had been fed toads or their mother carried high concentrations of the compounds.” The snake therefore does not make the toxins; it gets them from toads, either by eating them or through its mother.

B.why_wrong: Snakes from localities without toads “lacked the toxins in their neck glands entirely,” so they do not make their own.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares the amounts of toxin in hatchlings and in their mothers.

D.why_wrong: A mother’s toxins explain why some unfed hatchlings had toxins; the text says nothing about toxins being needed to digest toads.

sources.what: Hutchinson et al. 2007, PNAS (PubMed abstract): Rhabdophis tigrinus nuchal glands hold bufadienolides; snakes from toad-free localities lack them; hatchlings had them only if fed toads or born to a dam with high concentrations; the toxins are sequestered from dietary toads

items.notes: Area: natural science (herpetology, chemical ecology). S4 medium: two candidate sources (make or obtain), one ruled out by toad-free snakes and the feeding experiment, as in 2.17’s elimination. Distractors: REV, CMP, MIX (maternal toxins tied to digestion).

items.subtype: T5 evidential status: the traits cited for an early dog also occur in wolves
items.passage: A fossil canid skull more than 30,000 years old, recovered from Goyet Cave in Belgium, differs noticeably from the skulls of recent wolves. In 2009, paleontologist Mietje Germonpré’s research group identified it as one of the earliest known dogs, partly because it displays features thought to accompany domestication, such as a shortened snout. Such features, however, have also been documented in both ancient and modern wolves. The skull’s distinctive shape, therefore, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: establishes that dogs were domesticated in Belgium earlier than anywhere else.
indicates that the Goyet animal was more closely related to modern wolves than to modern dogs.
leaves open whether the animal was an early dog or a wolf with unusual features.
shows that shortened snouts appeared in wolves only after people had begun keeping dogs.
items.explanation: The skull was identified as a dog “partly because it displays features thought to accompany domestication,” but “such features, however, have also been documented in both ancient and modern wolves.” Since a wolf could show the same features, the shape alone cannot settle whether the animal was a dog or an unusual wolf.

A.why_wrong: The text casts doubt on whether the animal was a dog at all and says nothing about domestication anywhere else, so it cannot establish that Belgium came first.

B.why_wrong: The text shows only that the evidence for a dog is not decisive; it gives no evidence that the animal was closer to modern wolves.

D.why_wrong: The text says the features occur in “ancient and modern wolves” but never says when they first appeared in wolves.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Paleolithic dog: the Goyet canid (about 36,000 years ago) differed from recent wolves and was identified in 2009 as a Paleolithic dog; shortened rostrum and tooth crowding, used to propose such dogs, are documented in both ancient and modern wolves, and the specimens may be a divergent wolf population

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology, domestication). S5 medium: evidence for a claim (dog-like skull) plus an equally good rival (wolves show the same features) leads to a hedged conclusion. Options avoid the official 2.18 shapes (“is not conclusive evidence,” “eliminates,” “would be difficult to account for”). Age given as “more than 30,000 years” because the sources date it to 31,680 and about 36,000 years.

items.subtype: T1 conditional: a small and a large change to a default have unequal effects, so influence depends on size
items.passage: A default is the option that takes effect when a person makes no active choice, and defaults are known to influence decisions in numerous settings. During one winter, researchers led by Zack Brown lowered the default thermostat settings in an office building of the OECD, an intergovernmental economic organization, while leaving employees free to adjust the temperature themselves. Lowering the default by 1°C reduced employees’ chosen temperatures more, on average, than lowering it by 2°C did, and employees who had frequently adjusted their thermostats before the experiment were less affected, suggesting that a default’s influence ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: grows steadily as the gap between the default and the setting people would otherwise choose becomes wider.
depends more on employees’ past habits than on how far the default is lowered, since frequent adjusters were less affected.
may weaken once a default strays so far from what people find comfortable that they override it.
is greatest among the people who are most accustomed to choosing settings for themselves.
items.explanation: Lowering the default by 1°C “reduced employees’ chosen temperatures more, on average, than lowering it by 2°C did,” and employees who had “frequently adjusted their thermostats” were “less affected.” A larger change produced a smaller effect, which suggests that a default that strays too far from what people find comfortable prompts them to change it, weakening its influence.

A.why_wrong: A 2°C change, the wider gap, reduced chosen temperatures less than a 1°C change, so influence did not grow with the gap.

B.why_wrong: Frequent adjusters were indeed “less affected,” but the size of the change also mattered (a 1°C cut did more than a 2°C cut), and the text gives no way to compare the two influences, so it cannot say that habits count for more.

D.why_wrong: Employees who “frequently adjusted their thermostats” were “less affected,” so the default’s influence was weaker, not greater, among them.

sources.what: Brown, Johnstone, Hascic, Vong, Barascud 2013, Energy Economics (RePEc abstract): randomized winter test of default thermostat settings at the OECD; small decreases (1 degree) led to a greater reduction in chosen settings than large decreases (2 degrees); occupants more apt to adjust before were less susceptible

items.notes: Area: social science (behavioral economics). S7: two changes of different size with unequal effects lead to a conditional; two steps (a bigger change did less; together with habitual adjusters being less affected, people override defaults that stray too far). The overriding mechanism is the key’s inference, not a passage fact, as in the source. Distractors: REV, VAR (office size, reported in the paper but not in the passage), MIX.

fixes: B (VAR, office size; off-topic) replaced by a PART option that keeps the true habit finding and ranks it above the size of the change without support

band7.why: Two steps (a bigger cut did less, and habitual adjusters were less affected; so people override a default that strays too far). After the fix B keeps a true premise and adds an unsupported ranking; A and D are reversals each answered by one reported result. Key is a hedged conditional. Band 6.

items.subtype: T1 conditional: two mating tactics favour opposite forms, so the value of horns depends on tactic
items.passage: In the dung beetle Onthophagus taurus, males exceeding a critical body size develop a pair of long, curved horns, whereas smaller males remain hornless. Females reproduce in tunnels excavated beneath dung, and biologists Armin Moczek and Douglas Emlen observed that horned males aggressively defend tunnel entrances against competitors, with longer-horned males more likely to prevail. Hornless males instead attempt to sneak past guarding males to reach females, a tactic demanding considerable maneuverability in narrow tunnels. When the researchers compared males of identical body size, horned individuals moved through tunnels less nimbly than hornless ones. Taken together, these observations suggest that horns ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: enable males to excavate deeper tunnels than hornless males are able to dig.
would benefit even small males if those males chose to guard tunnel entrances.
improve a male’s agility inside tunnels, provided that the horns are relatively short.
may help or hinder a male, depending on how he competes for access to females.
items.explanation: Horned males “aggressively defend tunnel entrances,” and “longer-horned males” are “more likely to prevail,” so horns aid fighting. But sneaking demands “considerable maneuverability,” and horned males “moved through tunnels less nimbly than hornless ones,” so horns hamper sneaking. Whether horns help therefore depends on which tactic a male uses.

A.why_wrong: The text never says males dig tunnels or compares how deep horned and hornless males can dig.

B.why_wrong: The text says only males above “a critical body size” grow horns and never reports small males guarding entrances, so it gives no basis for this claim.

C.why_wrong: Horned males of the same body size “moved through tunnels less nimbly” than hornless ones, so horns reduced agility rather than improving it.

sources.what: Moczek and Emlen 2000, Animal Behaviour (PubMed abstract): Onthophagus taurus males above a critical size grow horns, smaller males are hornless; horned males defend tunnel entrances and longer horns win fights; hornless males sneak, which needs manoeuvrability; horns reduce agility in tunnels at equal body size

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior, evolution). S7 medium: two tactics with opposite needs lead to a conditional (“depending on how he competes”), like 3.14’s “depending on the crabs’ location.” Distractors: OUT (digging), EXT (small males), REV (agility).

items.subtype: T1 link: a skeletal condition common among the crew and among modern archers
items.passage: The Mary Rose, a warship that served King Henry VIII, sank off the southern coast of England in 1545. Centuries later, archaeologists raised the ship and examined the skeletons of many of its crew members. Because the ship carried hundreds of longbows, a large share of the men on board were probably archers. Researchers discovered that an unusually high number of the skeletons show os acromiale, a condition affecting the shoulder blade that is also common among modern archers who train intensively. This evidence suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the Mary Rose sank because its archers were unable to draw their longbows.
practicing with longbows may have caused the shoulder condition in many crew members.
sailors on the Mary Rose were more likely than the archers on board to have problems with their shoulders.
modern archers use longbows more often than they use other kinds of bows.
items.explanation: Many of the men were “probably archers,” and “an unusually high number of the skeletons show os acromiale,” a condition “also common among modern archers who train intensively.” The condition shows up wherever there is heavy archery training, so practicing with longbows may have caused it in many of the crew.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no cause for the sinking and never says the archers could not draw their bows.

C.why_wrong: The condition is linked to archery, so the text points to the archers, not other sailors, as the ones more likely to have it.

D.why_wrong: The text says modern archers who train hard often have the condition, but it never says which kinds of bows they use.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Mary Rose: sank 1545, raised in the modern excavation; about 250 longbows aboard, many crew likely archers; a disproportionate number of skeletons show os acromiale, known among modern elite archers and caused by stress on the arm and shoulder

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S8 easy: two co-occurrences (archers aboard, condition in the skeletons; condition in modern archers) lead to a link, like 1.7’s fur gene and immunity. Distractors: OUT, REV, OUT.

items.subtype: T2 belief: what workers’ paying for a practice reveals about how they valued it
items.passage: Rolling cigars by hand is skilled but repetitive work. Beginning in 1865, cigar makers in Cuba found a way to make their long workdays less monotonous: they hired a lector, or reader, who sat in the factory and read newspapers and books aloud while they worked. The workers themselves, rather than the factory owners, hired and paid the lector. The custom later spread to cigar factories in Ybor City, a neighborhood in Tampa, Florida, and it continues in Cuba today. The workers’ willingness to pay for the readings suggests that they ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: hoped to learn to read newspapers printed in other languages.
were required by the factory owners to listen to the readings.
preferred working in Florida to working in Cuba.
found the readings valuable enough to spend their own money on them.
items.explanation: The text says “the workers themselves, rather than the factory owners, hired and paid the lector,” who read aloud to make their workdays “less monotonous.” People who pay for something out of their own earnings must think it is worth the cost, so the workers clearly valued the readings.

A.why_wrong: The text never mentions newspapers in other languages or workers learning to read; the readings were meant to make the work less monotonous.

B.why_wrong: The workers, “rather than the factory owners,” hired the lector, so the readings were the workers’ own choice.

C.why_wrong: The text says the custom spread to Florida and continues in Cuba, but it never compares how workers felt about the two places.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Lector (cigar manufacture): a reader hired by fellow workers to read books or newspapers aloud; began in Cuba in 1865 to relieve boredom; spread to Ybor City, Tampa; continues in Cuba

items.notes: Area: humanities and history (labor, reading culture). S9 easy: an action (workers paying for a reader) reveals what they valued, like 1.11’s gatherings that let Johnson get feedback. Distractors: OUT, REV, CMP.

items.subtype: T2 belief: a company’s choice of performers reveals what it knew about its recordings
items.passage: Between 1915 and 1925, the Thomas A. Edison company staged public recitals called tone tests, in which a singer performed alongside a phonograph playing the company’s Diamond Disc recording of that same singer. Periodically the singer would fall silent while the recording continued, and at the conclusion the lights were dimmed so the singer could depart unobserved, leaving audiences to determine whether they had been listening to a person or to a machine. Edison selected singers partly for their ability to imitate the sound of their own recordings, suggesting that the company ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: wanted audiences to notice the moments when the singer fell silent and the recording continued alone.
recognized that its recordings did not fully reproduce the natural sound of a singer’s voice.
dimmed the lights mainly to conceal how much louder the phonograph was than the singer.
expected singers who could imitate their recordings to sell more records than other singers would.
items.explanation: The recitals were meant to leave audiences unsure “whether they had been listening to a person or to a machine,” and Edison chose singers for “their ability to imitate the sound of their own recordings.” If the recordings had matched a natural voice, no imitation would have been needed; choosing singers who could sound like the record suggests the company knew its recordings differed from a singer’s unaltered voice.

A.why_wrong: The tests were built so the audience could not tell singer from machine; the singer even left “unobserved,” so noticing the switch was what the company hoped to avoid.

C.why_wrong: The lights were dimmed “so the singer could depart unobserved”; the text says nothing about the phonograph being louder than the singer.

D.why_wrong: The text never discusses record sales by different singers; the singers were chosen to make the comparison with the recordings succeed.

sources.what: Library of Congress, Now See Hear! blog (2015), Is It Live or Is It Edison?: tone-test recitals 1915 to 1925; the artist stopped and only the recording played; lights lowered so the performer left the stage in the dark; singers chosen for their ability to imitate the sound of their own recordings

items.notes: Area: humanities (history of recorded music). S9, T2: the company’s choice of performers reveals a belief; two steps (singers were chosen to sound like the record; so a natural voice and the record differed). Distractors: REV (notice the switch), CAUSE (lights hid loudness), OUT (record sales). The CID w3 claim on tone tests was withdrawn before writing, so the subject is unused.

band7.why: Two steps (singers were chosen to sound like their records; so the records differed from a natural voice). A reverses the aim of the test, C misreads the dimmed lights, D an OUT on sales; key inferred, not echoed. Band 6.

items.subtype: T4 purpose: a brood parasite’s laying habit exploits its host’s rejection rule
items.passage: The cuckoo finch of Africa never raises its own young; instead, it lays its eggs in other birds’ nests, most frequently those of the tawny-flanked prinia, which raises the finch’s chicks as its own unless it identifies and rejects the foreign eggs. Prinias reject eggs that differ in appearance from their own, but Martin Stevens, Jolyon Troscianko, and Claire Spottiswoode discovered that as the proportion of foreign eggs in a nest increases, prinias become less inclined to reject them and require more substantial differences before doing so. Individual cuckoo finch females frequently deposit multiple eggs in the same prinia nest, a behavior that most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: allows the finch to lay eggs that more closely resemble those of the prinia.
makes it easier for prinias to distinguish their own eggs from foreign ones.
improves the odds that the prinia will raise the finch’s young instead of rejecting them.
ensures that at least one finch chick survives competition with its nestmates.
items.explanation: The researchers found that “as the proportion of foreign eggs in a nest increases, prinias become less inclined to reject them.” A finch that lays several eggs in one nest raises that proportion, so the habit most likely makes the prinia more willing to keep and raise the finch’s eggs.

A.why_wrong: Laying more eggs changes how many foreign eggs a nest holds, not how closely each egg resembles the prinia’s.

B.why_wrong: More foreign eggs make prinias “less inclined to reject them,” so the habit makes distinguishing harder for the host, not easier.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about competition among chicks; it links the number of foreign eggs to whether the prinia rejects them.

sources.what: Stevens, Troscianko, Spottiswoode 2013, Nature Communications (PubMed abstract): tawny-flanked prinia is the main host of the cuckoo finch; hosts reject eggs that differ from a template, but as the proportion of foreign eggs rises they reject less and need larger differences; repeated parasitism by the same female is common and likely an adaptation to increase acceptance

items.notes: Area: natural science (ornithology, coevolution). S9 medium: a parasite’s behaviour read for its purpose; two steps (several eggs raise the foreign share; a higher share lowers rejection). Distractors: MIX (resemblance), REV (host discrimination), CAUSE (chick competition).

removed.reason: Subject collision: official CoE item 8584f3ce (band 7) is sea otters and the health of eelgrass meadows (Foster, Vancouver Island); this item is sea otters helping eelgrass at Elkhorn Slough. Same organisms, same question; not reworked in review.

Topic-fame tell: the New York cabdriver income-targeting study (Camerer et al. 1997) is a behavioral-economics staple, and the key (fewer extra hours than the models predict) restates its headline finding, so knowing the study picks the key; the policy wrapper adds no step.
